Faire face à la discrimination raciale d: Confronting Racial Discrimination in the Health Care System
« Le système de santé a été créé sur des: “The health care system was built on racist foundations...”
La mort de Mireille Ndjomouo, le 7 mars: The death of Mireille Ndjomouo on March 7 shook the entire province. She died two days after posting a video in which she denounced the treatment she was receiving at Charles-Lemoyne hospital in Longueuil. The case is still under investigation. Recently, several Indigenous patients have complained of mistreatment. Barely six months after the death of Joyce Echaquan at Saint-Charles-Borromée hospital in Joliette, this event has reopened old wounds. Although it is still unclear what happened during Ms. Ndjomouo’s hospital stay, the tragedy has started a conversation about racism in hospitals.
L’histoire de Mireille Ndjomouo, comme c: The stories of Mireille Ndjomouo and Joyce Echaquan hit Ismaëlle Rose like a punch to the gut. They bring back the painful memory of a major operation she underwent last June at Maisonneuve-Rosemont hospital. “I had to recover not only from the surgery, but also from the violence I went through,” she says of her hospitalization. Her two-month convalescence was compounded by post-traumatic shock, which forced the 43-year-old woman to interrupt her studies. “I don’t know how or why I’m alive!” she exclaims, recalling her hospital stay. This was not Ismaëlle’s first procedure for a recurring health problem. This one, however, turned out to be very different from the earlier ones. The young woman says that when she woke up, she was hit by unbearable pain. She was reportedly left in that state for an entire day before being given epidural medication for relief. Later, a nurse checked on her. The nurse reportedly said: “Do you remember me? I was beside you all day after your operation, I had to fight to get your pain treated. In the end, you were in agony,” Ismaëlle recounts, still deeply traumatized.
La patiente a été à la charge de plusieu: The patient was in the care of several health care workers during the six days she spent in hospital. She believes that several of them took good care of her. Ismaëlle also describes a number of other incidents and problems that she says afflicted her during her stay: a broken call button that staff refused to check, malnutrition, an allergic reaction that was not taken seriously, medication administered irregularly. Each time, she says, she tried to report it so the situation could be corrected. “I was treated horribly, I was insulted, I was told it was all in my head,” she says of some hospital staff members. Before she was discharged, a member of the nursing staff tried to make her feel guilty. “I was told that nobody liked going into my room, that the doctors talked about me among themselves, that I was a difficult patient,” she says. “Yet I was extremely weak for most of my stay.” Ismaëlle wonders what could have led some hospital staff members to behave this way. “I feel like misogyny is at play, and I don’t rule out racism,” she says. With the pandemic raging, the young woman was not allowed to have anyone with her during her hospital stay. “There were no witnesses, no loved ones; that can play a role in how people behave,” she believes. This is the first time she has told this story. “We know that nobody is going to believe us, that they’ll say we’re exaggerating,” she laments. “It’s only recently that we’ve been hearing about this kind of thing.”
« On entend beaucoup ce type d’histoire: “We hear a lot of stories like this in racialized communities,” says Ariane Métellus, a perinatal consultant. “When you experience racism, you know it, you feel it. But how do you explain it to someone? We heard about these incidents because they were filmed,” she continues. “What about when they aren’t?”
La spécialiste en périnatalité voit de f: The perinatal specialist sees it as a positive sign that more and more people are choosing to share their experiences. “There’s a taboo. Before, we didn’t talk about people who experience violence and racism in the medical system,” observes Ms. Métellus. In her work, she conducts research, offers training and examines the procedures followed in hospitals. It was her own experience that pushed her to start her practice, first as a birth doula. Her first delivery left a bitter taste. “A doctor told me: ‘You Black women have a small pelvis, so it often ends in a C-section,’” she recounts.
Ariane Métellus évoque d’autres croyance: Ariane Métellus brings up other unfounded beliefs that persist, the existence of which several other professionals interviewed for this report confirm. There is what’s known as “Mediterranean syndrome,” a racist stereotype according to which Arab, Black or racialized people exaggerate their symptoms and pain. Care and treatment can be greatly affected as a result. The specialist also points to erroneous theories claiming that Black people feel less pain. She herself, like Ismaëlle, believes this misconception may have played a role in the treatment she received during her hospitalization. “The health care system was built on racist foundations. For example, the father of modern gynecology practised and experimented on Black slaves. Some things carry on,” the perinatal consultant tells us. She believes that prejudice and racism do not spare health care professionals, even though they take an oath to practise. “There are individuals who are racist in their everyday lives, and those individuals work in this system,” says Ms. Métellus. She explains that racism can also be systemic, meaning that structures and practices can result in some people receiving inadequate treatment.
Selon la consultante en santé sexuelle e: According to the sexual and reproductive health consultant, it is even harder to raise the issue and make the case without numbers to back it up. In the meantime, we have to rely on the situation in the United States or Europe to form hypotheses about the experiences of certain population groups. “It’s not because it doesn’t exist or because these are isolated cases,” she says of differential treatment. She cites the United States as an example, where, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Black women are 243 per cent more likely to die from pregnancy- or childbirth-related causes than white women. It is one of the largest health disparities. There is still no data on this in Quebec, but several independent researchers are currently looking into the question. “If it’s happening there, among our neighbours, why would Quebec and Canada be exempt?” asks the perinatal consultant. “The problem can be solved when we talk about it seriously, when we give a voice to the people who experience violence and when we believe them,” she says.
Des patients traités différemment, la Dr: Dr. Alexandra Bastiani, an interventional cardiologist, regularly sees patients being treated differently. “I’ve seen situations where people make comments, commit microaggressions or behave in certain ways,” says the specialist. As a Black woman, she says she is sensitive to this kind of conduct and adds that she has received disparaging remarks from patients, but also from colleagues. The cardiologist remains cautious all the same, pointing out the gruelling work that hospital staff do every day. “I don’t want to turn a blind eye to what’s going on,” she says of this type of incident, which she considers to be systemic racism. “We have the knowledge, but we need to be able to provide adequate responses,” she believes. “It’s not a knowledge problem, it’s a perception problem,” the physician continues, before adding that a Black person is less likely to leave the hospital after a heart attack than a white person. Dr. Bastiani would like training on racism in hospital settings to be built into the medical school curriculum.
Le Dr Samir Shaheen-Hussain, urgentologu: Dr. Samir Shaheen-Hussain, a pediatric emergency physician, observes the effects of social injustice on patients’ health. He writes about it in his latest book, Fighting for a Hand to Hold: Confronting Medical Colonialism against Indigenous Children in Canada. In it, the pediatrician lays out systemic racism and its impact on the delivery of care in Quebec and Canada. He believes that the culture in which the health care system operates is strongly influenced by ideas of white supremacy and patriarchy. “Injustices don’t come out of nowhere. They are created by people and by the systems we live in.” The physician supports the practice of cultural safety, an approach that, in his view, can make a difference in the health care system. “This concept teaches practitioners and health care providers to understand the power dynamics inherent in health care and to reverse them, to recognize the dignity of the person they are treating, as well as their history and their social and political context,” explains Dr. Shaheen-Hussain, who is also an assistant professor at McGill University’s Faculty of Medicine. He believes that if health care professionals better understand the role of history and power dynamics, there is hope that this awareness can influence the type of care they provide. “If this initiative is properly implemented, the benefits will be felt by everyone. The lessons learned could apply to all kinds of people: Indigenous, Black, migrant and LGBTQ+ communities, and more.”
